title: Humphrey's Wobbly Boat Promise
markdown:
Humphrey Alpaca treated the veranda of the Puddlebrook Inn as a dry dock for ideas. Charcoal lived in the curl of his hoof. Parchment took the afternoon sun, the smell of honeysuckle, and a rumour of scones from the kitchen. He drew galleons with sails that had never met weather, sloops with ebony hulls, and once a submarine shaped like a sea serpent that would have startled any honest fish. He nodded at his own lines. The sparrows, busy in the ivy, did not contradict him.

His hooves were sure on grass. They were surer still on paper, where buoyancy was a matter of shading and a keel could be rubbed out with a thumb. Guests drifted past with teacups. Humphrey offered them a view of theoretical magnificence and accepted their admiration as if it were a tide table.

Then he remembered Lily.

The innkeeper’s daughter had a birthday that ended at sunset, and weeks ago, among clinking china and a summer breeze, Humphrey had promised her a boat fit for the Puddlebrook itself. Not a diagram. A boat. The thought arrived like a cold splash down a woolly neck. He could sketch a thousand ways to build. He had never, with his own hooves, asked wood to float.

A tremor ran through his coat. The polished boards of the veranda felt suddenly less like a studio and more like a stage he had booked without learning the part.

“A boat!” he said, too loudly, to a chair that had not asked. “Of course. For Lily. At once.”

Sketches scattered like leaves that had lost their tree. He made for the boathouse by the water, a weathered box he had only ever admired from a polite distance. Inside waited damp timber, old oil, coils of rope gone grey, and a fishy honesty his veranda never practised. The sun had already begun its unhelpful descent, a clock with no manners.

He flung the door wide. Cobwebs shivered. A spider reconsidered its afternoon.

“Diagram Alpha-Seven-Niner,” Humphrey announced, as if naming the sketch might persuade the lumber. The parchment showed a graceful curve, a thatched roof for shade, and a sail that looked suspiciously like butterfly wings. He gathered planks. He chose tools as if choosing them were the same as knowing them. A hammer. A saw. Nails that shone with unused confidence.

The first nail bent at an angle that no diagram had predicted. The second refused the wood altogether and lay on the floor like a sulk. He sawed. The plank splintered into a dozen jagged opinions. Sweat found his brow, uninvited. A line that had been elegant in charcoal became a sulk of lumber with a personality and no keel.

He held a plank that declined to be a hull and pictured himself returning to Lily with a speech about the seasonal shortage of butterfly-wing canvas. The speech was ready. It even had a beginning about unforeseen difficulties.

A small shadow detached itself from a heap of rope.

“Perhaps,” said Jun, in a voice like dry leaves, “a slightly different approach?”

Humphrey nearly dropped the plank. Jun the weasel spent his days tidying and mending. He saw the world in knots that held and hammers that fitted. Humphrey had almost told him to leave genius alone. Then he looked at the lopsided pile, the growing shadows in the doorway, and the sun’s rude hurry, and the speech died in his throat.

Jun pointed at a hammer whose head had not been used as a philosophical instrument. Humphrey grunted. The right nail, when offered the right angle, consented to enter. Jun’s paws found twine that remembered how to be useful. Humphrey held, and sawed more slowly, and discovered that wood had a grain that preferred to be asked.

They worked. It was not the serene triumph of a finished sketch. It was a scramble with sawdust in it. Bits of wood began, grudgingly, to agree with other bits of wood. Jun tied a joint that did not boast and did not fail. Humphrey stopped announcing diagram numbers and started listening for the sound of a nail that had gone in true.

By the first blush of sunset a shape sat on the dock: a hull of sorts, a mast, a deck that would not have passed any inspection except hope. Humphrey gave it a shaky hoof-shake and declared it almost ready. The Puddlebrook winked. He chose to take that as applause.

He nudged the thing into the water.

It listed like a tired duck. A gap near the waterline gurgled and spat a silver mouthful onto the boards. The brook, which had seemed so decorative from the veranda, announced itself as a critic. Humphrey’s heart performed a drop that no pencil could shade away.

Lily arrived with a face prepared for magnificence. The face faltered. She saw the uneven seams, the tilt, the little fountain of failure. Humphrey felt shame tighten in his throat, dry as discarded charcoal. He could still have offered the speech. He looked at Jun, who offered no verdict, only patience and a rummage already begun, and then at Lily, and the grand diagrams thinned to one usable sentence.

“Lily,” he said, the boom gone out of him, “I made a promise I did not quite know how to keep.”

She looked from the leaky boat to his face to Jun, who had found a tin of sealant and a square of canvas in a corner that believed in leftovers. A small smile arrived, practical as a patch.

“It can float,” she said. “That is the main thing. And it has a mast.”

Jun worked the gap with sticky competence. Humphrey held the canvas taut while the weasel’s paws pressed the worst of the honesty back into the hull. They reinforced the seams. Damp wood, tarry smell, the last of the light lying flat on the water. When they launched again the boat bobbed, and wobbled, and did not sink. Humphrey pushed it toward Lily with a smile that had not been rehearsed on parchment. She stepped in as if wobble were a kind of weather you could learn.

The next morning he sat on the veranda again. Charcoal ready. Honeysuckle still about its business. Dew on the grass like a second, quieter brook. He began a sketch of something splendid, then stopped before the sails could get ideas.

Jun was sorting loose threads from a guest’s scarf, brow furrowed as if the threads had opinions.

“Jun,” Humphrey said, without bluster, “about that hull for the new inn sign. Which way should the grain run if we want it to hold?”

Jun looked up. He did not make a speech. He tipped a paw toward a scrap of wood left from the night’s adventure. Humphrey set the charcoal down long enough to feel the grain with the pad of his hoof, the way a boat might, if it were ever asked. The veranda was still a studio. It had also, overnight, become a place where a question could arrive before a flourish.
characters: Humphrey (overconfident alpaca boat builder), Jun (weasel friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
